description: Caparra was a Roman city in Extremadura, Spain, originating as a pre-Roman Veton settlement in the province of Lusitania. Its most iconic monument is a tetrapylum -- a unique four-sided arch, the only surviving example in Spain -- erected at the end of the 1st century AD at the junction of the city's cardo and decumanus. The city gained municipal status under Emperor Vespasian's Edict of Latinity in 74 AD. Strategically located on the Via de la Plata connecting Emerita Augusta to Asturica, Caparra prospered through trade and agriculture. The site preserves remains of thermal baths, a forum with basilica and curia, three necropolises, residential quarters, and an amphitheatre. The city declined in the 4th century and was gradually abandoned.
name: Ciudad Romana de Cáparra

description: Enkomi was a pivotal Late Bronze Age urban centre near Famagusta in eastern Cyprus, active from approximately 1650 to 1050 BC. The city served as a major copper smelting and export hub with trade connections across the eastern Mediterranean, particularly to Ugarit. A 1375 BC tablet from Pharaoh Akhenaten references the Alashiya king's copper, strengthening the identification of Enkomi as Alasiya's capital. French and Cypriot expeditions (1934-1974) revealed ashlar architecture, rich chamber tombs containing gold diadems and silver cups, and significant Cypro-Minoan tablets. The city was overrun by the Sea Peoples around 1200 BC and finally abandoned after an earthquake c. 1050 BC.
name: Enkomi

description: Hattusa, near modern Bogazkale in north-central Turkey, was the capital of the Hittite Empire in the 2nd millennium BC and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Spanning approximately 180 hectares, the city was enclosed by 6.6 km of fortification walls with monumental gates including the famous Lion Gate and King's Gate. The site contains a large temple district, the Buyukkale acropolis, and the nearby rock sanctuary of Yazilikaya with its remarkable relief carvings of gods and goddesses. Excavations since 1906 have yielded thousands of cuneiform tablets in Hittite and Akkadian that documented the empire's administration and diplomacy.
name: Hattusas

description: The Tarxien Temples are a complex of four megalithic structures in Malta, built between 3600 and 2500 BC during the late Neolithic and reused in the Early Bronze Age as a cremation cemetery after 2000 BC. Discovered in 1913 by farmer Lorenzo Despott, excavations were led by Sir Themistocles Zammit from 1915 to 1919. The highly decorated South Temple features bas-relief sculptures of spirals and domesticated animals, and the lower portion of a colossal statue of a skirted figure. The Central Temple is unique in Malta for its six-apse plan. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992, the temples have been protected by shelters since 2015.
name: Templos de Tarxien

description: Oldest oracle in Greece, located 22 km southwest of Ioannina in Epirus, where priests called the Selloi interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak tree to deliver the prophecies of Zeus. Over 4,200 lead question-tablets have been recovered, dating from the 6th to 2nd centuries BC. King Pyrrhus of Epirus made Dodona his religious capital around 290 BC, grandly rebuilding the Temple of Zeus and constructing a 17,000-seat theatre that remains well preserved today. The Naia festival held here featured athletic, musical, and dramatic contests. The oracle ceased in the 4th century AD under Theodosius.
name: Archaeological Site of Dodoni

description: Milefortlets were small Roman forts extending Hadrian's Wall defensive system along the Cumbrian coast from Bowness-on-Solway southward for at least 27 miles. Unlike milecastles on the Wall proper, these were linked by a wooden palisade rather than a stone wall, and lacked gateways through the frontier. Each milefortlet had two associated watchtowers. Milefortlet 21 at Crosscanonby was the first to be totally excavated, yielding Hadrianic-period pottery (AD 117-138), sandstone gaming boards, and ironwork. The system helped control movement across the Solway Firth estuary.
name: Milefortlet - Hadrians Wall

description: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, near modern Selcuk, was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. First built around 550 BC and funded by Croesus of Lydia, it was burned by Herostratus in 356 BC and rebuilt before its final destruction in 401 AD. The Greek poet Antipater of Sidon declared that its grandeur made all other wonders lose their brilliance. Rediscovered in 1869 by an expedition led by John Turtle Wood for the British Museum, today only a single reconstructed column marks the site.
name: The Temple of Artemis-Selçuk

description: The Asklepion of Kos is an ancient healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine [1]. Built in 357 BC, it served as one of the principal seats of the Asklepiadai, a hereditary order of priest-physicians who guarded medical knowledge [2]. The sanctuary gained worldwide fame through its association with Hippocrates and other renowned ancient physicians [1]. Pilgrims flocked here seeking both spiritual and physical healing, following traditions where patients slept in the temple to receive divine visions from Asclepius himself [3]. Today, the ruins lie near modern Kos town, preserving fragments of what was once a renowned center of ancient medicine.
name: Asklepion, Kos

description: Hegra (Mada'in Salih) is a Nabataean archaeological site in Al-Ula, Medina Province, Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom's largest settlement south of Petra. It features 111 monumental rock-cut tombs carved into sandstone, 94 with decorated facades, dating primarily from the 1st century BCE to 74 CE. The largest facade, Qasr al-Bint, stands 16 m high. A key crossroads on the incense trade route, Hegra became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
name: Madain Saleh

description: Sardinia hosts over 200 dolmens concentrated in the north-central part of the island, particularly around Nuoro, forming one of Western Europe's most important megalithic groups. Dating from the end of the 4th to the end of the 3rd millennium BC, these collective tombs feature rectangular or polygonal chambers of vertical orthostats covered by horizontal capstones, originally enclosed in earthen mounds. Notable examples include Sa Coveccada in Mores (3 m high, 5 m wide) and the dolmens at Pranu Muttedu near Goni. Entrances typically face southeast with sealed doorways.
name: Dolmens of Sardinia

description: Termantia, known today as Tiermes, is an archaeological site carved into sandstone hills in Montejo de Tiermes, Soria, Spain. Originally a Celtiberian Arevaci stronghold with a necropolis dating to the 6th century BCE, it allied with Numantia during the Celtiberian Wars. The Romans conquered it in 98 BCE under consul Titus Didius, who forced inhabitants to the plains. The site's defining feature is its rock-cut architecture, with rooms carved directly into sandstone cliffs, later overlaid with Roman elements including a 1st-century aqueduct capable of supplying 20,000 people. Dubbed the "Spanish Pompeii" by archaeologist Blas Taracena in the 1930s.
name: Termantia

description: The nuraghe is the primary megalithic structure of ancient Sardinia, built during the Nuragic civilization that flourished between 1900 and 730 BC[1]. More than 7,000 nuraghes have been catalogued across the island, though archaeologists estimate the original number exceeded 10,000[1].
name: Nuraghes of Sardinia

description: Rock-cut tombs at the ancient Carian city of Kaunos near Dalyan in southwestern Turkey, on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List since 2014. The earliest artefacts date to the 9th century BC, while the famous cliff-face tombs with temple-like facades date to the 5th-2nd centuries BC. Over 150 rock-cut tombs line the cliffs between Dalyan and Kaunos, with twenty featuring monumental Ionic temple facades including two columns, triangular pediments, and acroterion palm leaves. The tombs facing the Dalyan River date to the mid-4th century BC and likely held local royalty. Kaunos was a thriving port trading salt, salted fish, and pine resin before a malaria epidemic caused its final abandonment in the 15th century AD.
name: Caunos Tombs of The Kings

description: Dooey's Cairn, also known as Ballymacaldrack Court Tomb, is a Neolithic burial monument near Dunloy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland [1]. Named after Andrew Dooey, the landowner, the monument was transferred to state care in 1975 [2]. Court tombs, characteristic of the Neolithic period (c.4000-2000 BC), feature a semicircular courtyard leading to a burial chamber [3]. Approximately 400 court tombs exist in Ireland, with most concentrated in the northern regions [3].

description: Sanctuary of Hera at the tip of the Perachora peninsula on the Corinthian Gulf, founded in the 8th century BC. Two cult areas honoured Hera Akraia and Hera Limenia, with a 6th-century BC temple built over a 9th-century apsidal structure. Excavated by Humfry Payne for the British School at Athens in 1930-1933, the site yielded rich bronzes, terracottas, and ivories. An L-shaped stoa and agora were added in the 5th century BC, and a large cistern in the 4th century BC. The sanctuary declined after the Roman sack of Corinth in 146 BC.
name: Archaeological Site, Heraion

description: The Themistoclean Wall was completed in 479 BC under Athenian statesman Themistocles following the Persian Wars. It bisected the Kerameikos cemetery, incorporating funerary sculptures into its structure. Remnants are visible today at the Kerameikos archaeological site and beneath the Divani Palace Acropolis hotel.

description: The most sacred temple in the Inca Empire, originally built around 1200 AD as Inticancha and later magnificently renovated by Pachacutec, who renamed it Qorikancha ("golden enclosure"). The complex served as the religious, geographic, and political center of the Inca world, housing temples to Inti, Viracocha, and Quilla. Spanish conquistadors stripped the gold to ransom Atahualpa, and the Dominican order built the Church of Santo Domingo atop the ruins, though the original Inca stonework survived multiple earthquakes.

At nearly 30 metres long, 6 m wide, and 3.5 m high, it is one of the largest megalithic structures in Europe. Its 32 megaliths include roof stones weighing approximately 250 tonnes each. The passage uniquely aligns northeast toward the Pena de los Enamorados landmark, matching the summer solstice sunrise -- the only such dolmen alignment in continental Europe. description: The Biniai Nou hypogea are two Chalcolithic funerary tombs near Mahon on the island of Menorca, Spain, representing the oldest known buildings on the island. Their chambers are cut into bedrock, while the access corridors were constructed from vertical stone slabs forming megalithic facades. C14 dating of human bone from one hypogeum yielded a date of 2290-2030 BC, the earliest radiocarbon date in Menorcan prehistory. Excavations by a team from the Museum of Menorca recovered grave goods including ceramic vessels, bone awls, and radiolarite tool fragments, evidence of the island's first collective burial communities.
name: Biniai Nou Hypogea

description: The so-called Bosnian Pyramid of the Sun is Visocica Hill overlooking Visoko, Bosnia and Herzegovina, claimed since 2005 by businessman Semir Osmanagic to be the largest ancient pyramid on Earth. The hill is composed of Miocene-era sedimentary layers deposited 5-23 million years ago in an ancient lake system. Geologists identify it as a natural flatiron formation. The site once held the medieval Bosnian royal fortress of Visoki. Seven leading European archaeologists issued a declaration calling the pyramid project "a cruel hoax" with "no place in the world of genuine science," warning it was damaging real archaeological heritage.

It is the smallest of the three hills he named, standing about 120 m high and oriented eastward. Geologists and archaeologists have conclusively demonstrated that these hills are natural formations known as flatirons, composed of sandstone, clay, and siltstone deposited during the Miocene epoch. The European Association of Archaeologists formally condemned the claims as "a cruel hoax on an unsuspecting public". The site has no verified archaeological significance.

description: Birdoswald Roman Fort, known as Banna in antiquity, sits on a triangular spur above the River Irthing in Cumbria, towards the western end of Hadrian's Wall. Construction began in AD 122, initially in turf before being rebuilt in stone. The 2.14-hectare fort was garrisoned by the Cohors I Aelia Dacorum, a 1,000-strong infantry unit recruited from modern Romania, stationed here from c. 126 to 400 AD. Its defenses are the best preserved of any Wall fort. Uniquely, Birdoswald shows continuous occupation into the post-Roman period, with timber hall buildings replacing the granaries as the garrison evolved into a local warband.
name: Birdoswald Roman Fort

description: Enkomi (also known as Engomi) was a major Late Bronze Age city near Famagusta, Cyprus, occupied from approximately 1650 to 1050 BC. It functioned as a primary copper export hub with strong trade links to Ugarit and Egypt, and may have been the capital of the kingdom of Alasiya mentioned in the Amarna letters. The site features Cyclopean defensive walls, perpendicular street plans, and yielded the famous Ingot God and Horned God bronze statuettes. Excavations from 1896 to 1974 uncovered rich tombs with gold, silver, and ivory artifacts along with the highest concentration of Cypro-Minoan inscriptions on Cyprus. The city was abandoned around 1050 BC as Salamis rose to prominence.
name: Engomi Ancient City Ruins

description: Siega Verde is a Palaeolithic open-air rock art site in the province of Salamanca, Castile and Leon, Spain, preserving over 440 engravings on rocks eroded by the Agueda River. Discovered in the late 1980s by Professor Manuel Santonja Gomez, the carvings date from the Upper Palaeolithic (ca. 22,000-8,000 BCE) and depict animals including equids, aurochs, deer, goats, bison, reindeer, and woolly rhinoceros. In 2010, it was added as an extension to the Coa Valley Prehistoric Rock Art UNESCO World Heritage Site, together forming the most remarkable open-air Palaeolithic art ensemble on the Iberian Peninsula.

description: A 4th-century BC Lycian rock-cut tomb at ancient Telmessos (modern Fethiye, Turkey), carved into a cliff face to resemble a Greek temple facade with a triangular pediment and Ionic columns. The tomb interior contains a rectangular chamber with three stone benches (klinai) for burials. Named for Amyntas son of Hermapias, likely a local nobleman during the Achaemenid satrapy of Lycia. It is the largest of numerous rock tombs in the Fethiye cliffs.
name: Amyntas Rock Tombs
